items.title: 11.1 Structure and functioning of the heart

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and topic 11.1, printed pages 231-238: the pericardium, heart wall, chambers, valves, path of blood, cardiac cycle, heart sounds, conducting system, heart rate and the ECG.

blocks.text: Humans have two systems for the transport of materials to different parts of the body: the blood circulatory system and the lymphatic system. The closed blood circulatory system consists of blood, the heart and the blood vessels (arteries, capillaries and veins).

blocks.title: Recalling: blood
blocks.text: Blood is the medium in which dissolved nutrients, gases, hormones and wastes are transported throughout the body. It is composed of plasma and of cells or cell-like bodies (white blood cells, red blood cells, platelets). In a healthy person plasma is about 55% of the blood by volume and the cells about 45%.

The human heart is a hard-working pump that moves blood through the body. It is situated in the middle of the chest cavity, between the lungs; its back surface is near the vertebral column and its front surface behind the sternum and rib cartilages.
Pericardium

The heart is enclosed in a sac, the pericardium, which separates it from the surrounding organs. Its outer layer, the fibrous pericardium, is made of strong connective tissue; it protects the heart against external pressure and shocks and prevents its excessive dilation. Its inner layer, the serous pericardium, is itself a sac of two layers: the outer parietal pericardium beneath the fibrous pericardium, and the inner visceral pericardium (also called the epicardium), closely attached to the heart. The space between them, the pericardial cavity, contains up to 50 mL of pericardial fluid, which lubricates the heart and protects it from infections.
Wall of the heart

The wall of the heart has three layers. The inner layer of the pericardium, the epicardium, makes the outer lining of the wall. Beneath it is the thickest layer, the myocardium, made of cardiac muscle. Beneath the myocardium is the endocardium, a single layer of epithelial cells that makes the inner lining of the heart chambers.

blocks.title: Why the heart is felt on the left
blocks.text: The heart is usually felt on the left side because the left side of the heart is stronger and larger, since it pumps to all parts of the body. Because the heart lies between the lungs, the left lung is smaller than the right and has a cardiac notch in its border to accommodate it.
Chambers and valves of the heart

The heart has four chambers: two upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-walled ventricles. The atria receive blood from the body and pass it to the ventricles, which distribute it to the body. Atria and ventricles are separated by the atrioventricular septum; the two atria by the interatrial septum; and the two ventricles by the interventricular septum, which is much thicker than the interatrial septum. The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than that of the right ventricle, because it has to push the blood all over the body.

items: Atrioventricular valves, at the entrances of the ventricles in the atrioventricular septum: the tricuspid valve, of three cusps, between the right atrium and right ventricle, and the bicuspid or mitral valve, of two cusps, between the left atrium and left ventricle. When the ventricles contract these valves close and prevent backflow into the atria.

Semilunar valves (shaped like a half-moon), at the exits of the ventricles: the pulmonary valve at the base of the pulmonary artery and the aortic valve at the base of the aorta. When the ventricles relax these valves close and prevent backflow from the pulmonary artery and aorta into the ventricles.

blocks.text: Circulation of blood through the heart

The heart functions as a double pump, carrying out the pulmonary circulation (the supply of blood to the lungs) and the systemic circulation (the supply of blood to all the organs except the lungs). Complete separation of deoxygenated blood (right side) and oxygenated blood (left side) is maintained. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae and passes it to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve; when the right ventricle contracts, the blood passes through the semilunar pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries to the lungs. The oxygenated blood from the lungs is brought to the left atrium by the pulmonary veins and passes to the left ventricle through the bicuspid valve; when the left ventricle contracts, the blood passes through the aortic valve into the aorta, which carries it to all parts of the body except the lungs.

blocks.alt: A section of the heart. The superior and inferior venae cavae bring blue blood into the right atrium; it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. Pulmonary veins bring red blood into the left atrium; it passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle and through the aortic valve into the aorta. A septum divides the two sides. blocks.text: Cardiac cycle: the heartbeat

The heart works in continuous cycles. Its chambers relax and are passively filled with blood from the large veins, then contract and propel the blood through the body; these alternating relaxations and contractions are a cardiac cycle, or one heartbeat. While the atria are relaxed and filling, the ventricles are also relaxed: this relaxed period is diastole, during which both atria fill with blood. As blood accumulates in the atria their pressure rises and both contract, in atrial systole, passing the blood through the tricuspid and bicuspid valves into the two relaxed ventricles. When the ventricles are filled, both contract, in ventricular systole, pumping the blood into the pulmonary arteries and aorta; during ventricular systole the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close while the pulmonary and aortic valves open. In one complete heartbeat diastole lasts about 0.4 seconds, atrial systole about 0.1 seconds and ventricular systole about 0.3 seconds. In a lifetime the heart beats about 2.5 billion times without stopping.

blocks.text: Sounds of a heartbeat

When both ventricles contract together to pump blood into the pulmonary arteries and aorta, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close and the lubb sound is made. When ventricular systole ends and both ventricles relax, the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves close and the dubb sound is made; lubb-dubb can be heard with a stethoscope. If the valves do not close fully, or open narrowly, turbulence is created within the heart and can be heard as a heart murmur, which sounds like a hiss. Most murmurs are not serious; those that are can be corrected by replacing the damaged valves with artificial ones or with valves from an organ donor.
Control of the heartbeat (heart excitation and contraction)

The pumping of the heart is initiated by the sinoatrial node (SA node) or pacemaker, a small cluster of cardiac muscle cells embedded in the upper wall of the right atrium. The heartbeat starts when the SA node sends electrical impulses to the walls of the atria, making both contract simultaneously. The impulses then travel to the atrioventricular node (AV node), also a small cluster of cardiac muscle cells, at the lower portion of the interatrial septum. From the AV node the impulses reach the atrioventricular bundle, or bundle of His, a network of fibres in the interventricular septum; it divides into left and right branches, which end at the Purkinje fibres in the walls of the ventricles, and stimulation of these fibres makes the ventricles contract almost simultaneously. There is a delay of about 0.15 seconds in the conduction of impulses from the SA node to the AV node, permitting atrial systole to be completed before ventricular systole begins.

blocks.alt: A section of the heart with its conducting system: the SA node in the upper wall of the right atrium sends impulses to the AV node at the lower end of the atrial septum; from it the AV bundle runs down the septum and divides into a right branch and a left branch, which spread as Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls.

blocks.title: Artificial pacemaker
blocks.text: If the flow of electrical impulses is blocked, or the impulses from the SA node are weak, the rhythm of the heartbeat may be delayed or stopped. In such patients an artificial pacemaker, a battery-operated device surgically implanted near the AV node, emits electrical signals that trigger normal heartbeats.
Rate of heartbeat

The heart of an average adult beats about 70 times per minute and pumps the entire blood volume, about 5 litres, every minute. The normal speed is made and maintained by the pacemaker and AV node, but the brain also exerts some influence: during fever and exercise the control centre in the brain sends nerve signals to both the pacemaker and the AV node to increase the heart rate, to cope with the situation, and when we are asleep or at rest it slows their activity.
Electrocardiogram

The recording of the electrical potentials generated by the currents of cardiac impulses is the electrocardiogram (ECG). When a cardiac impulse passes over the surface of the heart a minute electrical current is generated, which spreads into the surrounding tissues and travels to the surface of the body. In an ECG the potentials generated by this current are measured and recorded by electrodes placed on the skin on opposite sides of the heart, attached to a machine, the electrocardiograph. The ECG helps to diagnose abnormalities in the conduction system of the heart and shows the following waves at specific events of the cardiac cycle.

items: P wave: the beginning of atrial depolarisation, initiated by the SA node, which causes atrial contraction. Irregular or absent P waves may indicate arrhythmia (lack of rhythmicity).
PR segment: the completion of atrial depolarisation, usually 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. A prolonged PR indicates a first-degree heart block.

QRS complex: the beginning of ventricular depolarisation; atrial repolarisation also occurs during this phase. Abnormalities may indicate bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia (a faster rate of contraction) or other ventricular abnormalities.

ST segment: the completion of ventricular depolarisation, ordinarily about 0.08 seconds. It can be depressed in ischaemia (decreased flow of blood and oxygen to the heart muscle) and elevated in myocardial infarction.
T wave: the beginning of ventricular repolarisation. T-wave abnormalities may indicate electrolyte disturbance; the hyper-acute T wave is the earliest finding of acute myocardial infarction.
QT interval: from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave, normally about 0.40 seconds.

blocks.title: The blood's journey
blocks.text: In an adult about 8,000 litres of blood move through 96,000 km of blood vessels every day.
